rw: Posting transfers amounts from the journal to the matching ledger accounts, which is how the ledger gets updated with every transaction after it is first recorded in the journal.

ww.Mailing invoices to customers monthly: Mailing invoices is a billing and sales task, not an accounting cycle step; invoices are source documents that are later journalized, not the act of posting itself.
ww.Printing the financial statements: Printing financial statements happens near the end of the accounting cycle, after posting, the trial balance and adjustments, so it is a reporting step and not posting.
ww.Writing the first entry from a receipt: Writing the first entry from a receipt describes journalizing, which comes before posting; posting only begins once the journal entry already exists and is ready to copy.

rw: The cycle starts by analyzing the source document, then journalizing the transaction, then posting the journal entry to the ledger accounts, so this is the correct order.

ww.Post, analyze, journalize: Posting before analyzing makes no sense, because you cannot post a transaction to the ledger until you have analyzed it and journalized it first, so this order fails.
ww.Journalize, close, post: Closing happens at the end of the cycle, after adjusting and the statements, so placing close second ahead of post breaks the sequence of the accounting cycle steps.
ww.Post, journalize, analyze: Posting and journalizing come before analyzing here, which is backwards because a transaction must first be analyzed to know which accounts and amounts to record.

rw: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, while cash basis records them only when cash is received or paid, which is the key timing difference.

ww.Cash basis requires double entry of all: Double entry is used under both cash and accrual methods, so requiring it is not what separates them; the real difference is timing of recognition for revenue and expenses.
ww.Cash basis records only assets and nothi: Both methods record assets and other accounts; cash basis is simply less complete and skips receivables and payables, so claiming it records only assets is not accurate.
ww.Accrual ignores unpaid bills; cash recor: This reverses the methods: accrual records unpaid bills as payables when incurred, while cash basis ignores them until cash is paid out to the vendor later on.

rw: Under accrual accounting revenue is recorded when earned, which is when the service was performed on March 28, even though the cash payment did not arrive until April 5.

ww.April 5: April 5 is when cash was received, which matters under cash-basis accounting, but accrual accounting records revenue when the service is performed, not when the money arrives.
ww.Both months: Revenue is recognized once, in the period it is earned; recording it in both March and April would double count the same $ sale and overstate total income.
ww.Either month: Accrual accounting follows the revenue recognition principle, which gives a definite answer; revenue cannot be placed in whichever month is convenient for the business owner.

rw: Accrual accounting matches expenses to the period in which they are incurred, so the electricity used in December is a December expense even though payment happens in January.

ww.Both months: An expense is recorded in one period only; splitting one December bill across December and January would double count the cost and overstate expenses overall for the two months.
ww.No month: Every expense must land in some period; the bill was incurred, so under accrual accounting it cannot belong to no month and simply be left out of the books.
ww.January: January is when the bill is paid in cash, which is the cash-basis answer; accrual accounting records the expense when the service was used or incurred, not when paid.

rw: A compound journal entry affects more than two accounts, with total debits still equal to total credits, such as a sale paid partly in cash and partly on credit.

ww.An entry that corrects a mistake: An entry that corrects a mistake is a correcting entry, not a compound entry; compound entries are defined by how many accounts they touch, not by their purpose.
ww.An entry that is repeated each month: An entry repeated each month is a recurring entry, such as monthly rent; being repeated does not make an entry compound, which depends on the number of accounts affected.
ww.An entry that earns interest each month: Interest-earning is unrelated to how an entry is structured; a compound entry is simply one that involves three or more accounts, not one that earns anything each month.

rw: The general ledger collects every account, such as cash, receivables and revenue, with running balances, so it is the central record used to prepare the trial balance and statements.

ww.To record the original source of each tr: The original source of each transaction is a source document like an invoice or receipt, while the journal is the book of original entry; the ledger holds summarized accounts.
ww.To list daily sales only, and nothing el: The ledger holds every account, not just sales, so limiting it to daily sales is wrong; daily sales are typically tracked in a sales journal or register.
ww.To store customer contact details and ad: Customer contact details belong in a customer master file or CRM system; the general ledger holds financial account balances, not names and addresses for mailing purposes.

rw: A contra account has a normal balance opposite its related account and offsets it, like Accumulated Depreciation reducing equipment or Sales Returns reducing sales revenue to a net figure.

ww.An account that is always zero or negati: A contra account can carry a normal balance opposite to its parent but is not always zero or negative; for example, Accumulated Depreciation normally has a credit balance of real size.
ww.An account used only by the auditors: Contra accounts are used by the company in routine bookkeeping, not only by auditors; examples such as Allowance for Doubtful Accounts appear in the regular ledger and statements.
ww.An account for owner withdrawals only: Owner withdrawals go in a Drawing account, which reduces equity, but that is a different equity account type and is not what the term contra account means in general.

rw: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts are temporary because they measure activity for one period, and their balances are closed to zero at period end so the next period starts fresh.

ww.Cash and accounts receivable balances: Cash and accounts receivable are assets, which are permanent accounts whose balances carry forward into the next period rather than being reset to zero by closing entries.
ww.Any account with a very small balance: An account is temporary because of its type and function, not because its balance is small; a tiny asset balance still carries over and remains a permanent account.
ww.Asset, liability and equity accounts: Asset, liability and equity accounts are permanent (real) accounts because their balances carry over from period to period and appear on the balance sheet, so they are not closed.

rw: Closing resets revenue, expense and drawing accounts to zero so each new period starts with a clean slate and income is measured only for that period, which is the purpose.

ww.So that they cannot be audited: Closing has nothing to do with preventing audits; closed accounts remain fully available in the records, and auditors still examine the closing entries along with everything else.
ww.To increase the cash balance owed: Closing does not raise any cash balance or create amounts owed; it only transfers temporary balances to equity, and cash is affected by actual receipts and payments instead.
ww.To remove assets from the ledger: Closing entries affect temporary accounts and equity, not assets; assets are permanent accounts that stay on the books and are never removed through the closing process.

rw: Net income of $52,000 less $41,500 is $10,500, and closing entries transfer that amount to Owner's Capital, increasing owner's equity by exactly the profit earned.

ww.Accounts payable: Accounts payable is a liability that changes with purchases on credit and payments, not with net income; closing entries do not touch it, so it is unaffected here.
ww.Total expenses: Total expenses are temporary account balances that are closed to zero, so they fall to zero after closing rather than increase by net income of $10,500.
ww.Cash on hand: Cash changes only through actual receipts and payments; closing entries are bookkeeping transfers between accounts and do not change the cash balance by the net income figure.

rw: Adjusting entries apply the matching principle, recording revenue earned and expenses incurred in the proper period even if cash has not moved, so the statements show accurate results.

ww.To close the revenue accounts to zero fi: Closing entries, not adjusting entries, bring revenue accounts to zero at period end, and they come after adjusting; adjustments exist to update accounts and not to clear them.
ww.To erase mistakes from the general journ: Mistakes are fixed with correcting entries, and erasing from the journal is poor practice; adjusting entries instead update accounts for accruals, deferrals and estimates at period end.
ww.To increase the cash account balance at: Adjusting entries are not meant to raise cash; they usually involve non-cash items like depreciation or accrued wages, and cash changes only when money actually moves.

rw: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life and is recorded by an adjusting entry at period end, since no outside transaction triggers it during the period.

ww.Purchasing a truck for cash: Buying a truck for cash is an ordinary transaction journalized when it happens, exchanging one asset for another, so it needs no period-end adjusting entry afterwards.
ww.Receiving a customer payment: Receiving a customer payment is a routine transaction recorded when it occurs; it is not an adjustment made at period end to bring accounts up to date.
ww.Paying the owner's draw: The owner's draw is an ordinary transaction recorded when cash is taken out; it is closed at period end but is not itself an adjusting item for the period.

rw: A prepaid expense is a cost paid in advance, like insurance or rent, recorded as an asset first and expensed gradually as the benefit is used up over later periods.

ww.A bill received but not yet paid in full: A bill received but not yet paid is an account payable or accrued expense, which is a liability; a prepaid expense is the opposite, with cash paid before use.
ww.Income received long before it is earned: Income received before it is earned is unearned revenue, a liability for the seller; a prepaid expense involves the business paying out cash, not receiving it.
ww.A cost that is never paid by the busines: A cost that is never paid would not be a prepaid expense; prepaid means the business has already paid cash in advance for a benefit to be received later.

rw: Unearned revenue is cash received before the service is performed or goods delivered, so it is a liability until earned, like a prepaid magazine subscription or gift card.

ww.Profit from the sale of old equipment: Profit from selling old equipment is a gain, which is reported as income; unearned revenue is a liability for cash received where the work has not yet been done.
ww.Revenue earned but not yet collected: Revenue earned but not yet collected is accrued revenue, an asset (receivable); unearned revenue is the reverse situation, where cash arrives before the work is done.
ww.Money borrowed from a lender or a bank: Money borrowed from a lender or bank is a loan, recorded as notes payable; unearned revenue arises from customer prepayments for goods or services, not from borrowing.

rw: Accrued revenue is revenue earned by performing work or delivering goods but not yet received in cash or recorded, so an adjusting entry records it as a receivable and revenue.

ww.Revenue collected in cash on the day of: Cash collected on the day of sale is ordinary current revenue that is already recorded; accrued revenue is earned but not yet collected, so nothing about it is same day.
ww.An expense paid in advance of its use by: An expense paid in advance is a prepaid expense, an asset; accrued revenue concerns income earned and not yet received, not costs paid ahead of use.
ww.Cash received for work that is not yet d: Cash received for work not yet done is unearned revenue, a liability; accrued revenue is the opposite, where the work is done but payment has not arrived yet.

rw: An accrued expense is incurred in the period but not yet paid or recorded, such as wages earned by employees at year end, so it is recorded as a payable.

ww.Income received early in the period: Income received early in the period is unearned or deferred revenue, a liability; an accrued expense concerns a cost the business owes, not income the business has received.
ww.An expense paid before it is used: An expense paid before it is used is a prepaid expense, an asset; accrued expenses are the reverse, where the cost has been used but cash is still owed.
ww.A cost permanently written off the books: A cost written off permanently describes a loss or expiry, not an accrual; an accrued expense is still owed and will be paid in cash at a later date.

rw: The matching principle requires recording the $1,200 as expense in December, so debit Wages Expense and credit Wages Payable, creating a liability until January payment is made.

ww.Debit Wages Payable and credit Cash now: Wages Payable is credited, not debited, when the liability is first recorded; debiting it and crediting Cash would imply cash was paid on December 31, which it was not.
ww.Debit Cash and credit Wages Expense now: Debiting Cash would increase cash, but no cash was received; the business owes wages, so the entry must record the expense and the liability, not a cash receipt.
ww.No entry until wages are paid in cash: Waiting until payment in cash would leave December expenses and liabilities understated; accrual accounting requires the adjusting entry at year end so the expense lands in December.

rw: $2,400 divided by 12 is $200 per month, times 3 months from October 1 to December 31 is $600 of insurance expense, leaving $1,800 as a prepaid asset.

ww.$1,200: $1,200 would cover six months of the policy, but only three months (October, November, December) have passed, so this overstates the expense for the year ended December 31.
ww.$200: $200 is one month of insurance ($2,400 divided by 12), but three months have been used by December 31, so this understates the expense for the period by a lot.
ww.$2,400: $2,400 is the full 12-month cost, which would only be expensed after a whole year; at December 31 just a quarter of the policy has expired and been used.

rw: $900 divided by six months is $150 per month, and one month of lessons (June) has been completed, so $150 is earned and the remaining $750 stays as unearned revenue.

ww.$900: $900 is the total prepayment for all six months; earning all of it would require the full six months of lessons to be completed, not just the first month.
ww.$450: $450 would be three months of lessons, but only one month (June) has passed, so this would overstate the revenue earned by June 30 by $300.
ww.$0: Cash was received, but revenue is earned as lessons are given; one month of lessons has been delivered by June 30, so earned revenue is $150, not zero.

rw: Depreciation spreads cost over time: debit Depreciation Expense to record the period's cost and credit Accumulated Depreciation, a contra asset, rather than reducing the Equipment account directly.

ww.Debit Equipment, credit Cash for the cos: Debiting Equipment and crediting Cash is the entry for buying an asset, not for depreciation; depreciation does not involve cash and does not add to the asset's cost.
ww.Debit Accumulated Depreciation, credit E: This debit would reduce a contra account and credit the Equipment account directly, which reverses the proper treatment; depreciation expense must be debited to show the cost used.
ww.Debit Cash, credit Depreciation Expense: Depreciation never involves cash; crediting Depreciation Expense would also reduce an expense instead of recording one, so this entry has both sides wrong for the purpose.

rw: Accrued wages expense records wages owed but unpaid, debiting Wages Expense and crediting Wages Payable, which is a new liability on the balance sheet at period end.

ww.Earning unearned revenue: Earning unearned revenue reduces a liability by moving it to revenue, so it removes a liability from the balance sheet instead of creating one.
ww.Using prepaid insurance: Using prepaid insurance moves cost from an asset to an expense, reducing assets; it does not create a liability on the balance sheet at all.
ww.Depreciation expense: Depreciation expense is recorded with a credit to Accumulated Depreciation, a contra asset that reduces assets; it does not create any liability on the balance sheet.

rw: Book value equals cost minus accumulated depreciation, so $9,000 minus $3,500 equals $5,500, which is the remaining undepreciated cost of the equipment on the books.

ww.$12,500: $12,500 adds the depreciation to the cost, but accumulated depreciation is subtracted from cost to get book value, so this is the wrong direction for the arithmetic.
ww.$9,000: $9,000 is the original cost of the equipment; book value is lower because $3,500 of accumulated depreciation has already been recognized against that asset over time.
ww.$3,500: $3,500 is only the accumulated depreciation to date, which is the amount already used up, not the remaining book value of the equipment still held on the books.

rw: The worksheet is an informal working paper that lays out the trial balance, adjustments and adjusted balances in columns, making statements easier to prepare accurately afterward.

ww.To record transactions as they happen da: Daily transactions are recorded in the journal as they happen; the worksheet is a period-end tool and is not part of the day-to-day recording of transactions.
ww.To replace the general ledger book entir: The worksheet is only a working paper and cannot replace the general ledger, which remains the formal permanent record of every account in the accounting system.
ww.To send to the bank as the final report: The worksheet is an internal working paper, not a formal report; the financial statements are what get shared with the bank and outside users, not the worksheet.

rw: The income statement comes first because net income is needed by the owner's equity statement, whose ending capital is then used on the balance sheet, so this order is correct.

ww.Owner's equity, balance sheet, then inco: The balance sheet needs the ending capital from the equity statement, and the equity statement needs net income first, so this order puts the steps out of sequence.
ww.Balance sheet, owner's equity, then inco: The balance sheet cannot be finished until the owner's equity statement gives ending capital, and that depends on net income, so the balance sheet cannot come first.
ww.Balance sheet first, then income stateme: Starting with the balance sheet fails because it depends on ending owner's equity, which depends on net income from the income statement; the flow runs in the opposite direction.

rw: Closing entries transfer revenue, expense and drawing balances into owner's equity (capital), resetting those temporary accounts to zero so the next period begins with a fresh start.

ww.To permanently delete old records of the: Closing entries do not delete anything permanently; they zero out temporary accounts, while old records are kept for audits, taxes and legal reasons for many years afterward.
ww.To correct errors in the general journal: Errors in the journal are fixed with correcting entries, not closing entries; closing is a routine end-of-period step, whether or not any mistakes were found earlier.
ww.To adjust asset values to match market p: Assets are recorded at historical cost and adjusted only by depreciation, never to market prices through closing entries, whose only job is resetting temporary accounts to zero.

rw: Income Summary is a temporary account used only during closing: revenues and expenses are moved into it, and its balance, the net income or loss, then goes to capital.

ww.Contra Asset: A contra asset account like Accumulated Depreciation is a permanent account that stays on the books; it is not used as the temporary holding account during the closing process.
ww.Unearned Revenue: Unearned Revenue is a permanent liability account whose balance carries forward to the next period, so it is not a clearing account used while closing the books.
ww.Receivables: Receivables are permanent asset accounts that carry forward; the clearing account used while closing is a temporary account created for the process, which is Income Summary.

rw: The first closing entry debits each revenue account for its balance and credits Income Summary, which brings the revenue accounts to zero and starts the transfer to equity.

ww.Close the cash account to Income Summary: Cash is a permanent asset account and is never closed; the closing process only involves temporary accounts such as revenue, expenses and drawing, plus Income Summary.
ww.Close the liabilities to expense account: Liabilities are permanent accounts that are not closed, and they would never be closed into expense accounts; closing only moves temporary account balances into Income Summary and capital.
ww.Close the owner's capital account first: Closing the capital account first is incorrect, because capital is permanent and is the final destination; revenue and expense accounts are closed through Income Summary before capital changes.

rw: After closing, only permanent accounts (assets, liabilities and owner's capital) have balances, so the post-closing trial balance lists just those, proving the ledger is ready for the next period.

ww.Every account, even closed: Closed accounts have zero balances, and only permanent accounts are listed; including every account, even revenue and expenses, would defeat the purpose of the post-closing trial balance.
ww.Only revenue accounts: Revenue accounts are temporary and have been closed to zero, so they do not appear with balances on the post-closing trial balance, which lists only permanent accounts.
ww.Only drawing accounts: Drawing accounts are temporary and closed to capital during closing, so they have zero balances and do not appear on a post-closing trial balance.

rw: The post-closing trial balance verifies that total debits equal total credits after closing entries have been posted, confirming the ledger is in balance before the next period starts.

ww.To calculate net income once more: Net income is calculated earlier, on the income statement and in the closing process; the post-closing trial balance does not recompute it, only checks account balances after closing.
ww.To record the next period's sales: Next period's sales are recorded as they occur in the new period; the post-closing trial balance is a check on the old period's closing, not a place for new transactions.
ww.To adjust depreciation at year end: Depreciation is adjusted before the statements are prepared, using adjusting entries; the post-closing trial balance comes after closing and does not make adjustments of any kind.

rw: A fiscal year is any 12-month period a business chooses for reporting, such as July 1 to June 30, which often fits a seasonal business better than the calendar year.

ww.The time between two audits each year: The time between audits is not what defines a fiscal year; a fiscal year is a 12-month accounting period, whether or not an audit happens at the end of it.
ww.A period that must start on January 1: A fiscal year can start on any date, such as July 1 or October 1; only a calendar year must start on January 1, so this is too restrictive.
ww.A period of exactly six months in length: Six months is a half-year, and a period of exactly six months would not be a fiscal year, which always covers a full twelve-month span used for reporting.

rw: Accumulated Depreciation is a permanent contra asset account, so its credit balance carries forward and appears on the post-closing trial balance after the temporary accounts are closed.

ww.Owner's Drawing account: The Owner's Drawing account is temporary and is closed to capital during the closing process, so it has a zero balance on the post-closing trial balance.
ww.Depreciation Expense account: Depreciation Expense is a temporary expense account closed to Income Summary at period end, leaving a zero balance, so it does not appear on the post-closing trial balance.
ww.Service Revenue account: Service Revenue is a temporary account that is closed to zero during the closing entries, so it does not carry a balance on the post-closing trial balance.

rw: Without the entry, revenue earned is not recorded, so revenue and net income are understated, and the missing receivable means assets are understated by the same amount of money.

ww.Expenses are overstated and assets too l: Omitting accrued revenue leaves revenue unrecorded, so revenue is understated rather than expenses overstated; the missing receivable also means assets are too low, not expenses too high.
ww.Revenue is overstated and liabilities un: Leaving out accrued revenue means revenue is understated, not overstated; the unrecorded amount is an asset, so liabilities are not affected by this particular omission.
ww.Only the cash balance is wrong on the bo: The omission affects revenue, net income, receivables and equity, not just cash; cash is unchanged because the accrued amount has not yet been received from the customer.

rw: Without the adjustment, insurance expense is left out, so expenses are understated and net income is overstated, while the prepaid insurance asset stays too high on the balance sheet.

ww.Expenses are overstated and assets under: Omitting the entry means the insurance expense is never recorded, so expenses are understated rather than overstated, and the prepaid asset stays too high instead of too low.
ww.Liabilities are understated and revenue: Prepaid insurance is an asset and the omission does not involve liabilities; the unrecorded expense also means revenue is unaffected, so neither of these effects follows from it.
ww.Revenue is overstated and equity is too: Revenue is unaffected by an unrecorded insurance expense; the actual effect is that expenses are understated, which makes net income and equity too high, but not revenue.

rw: Expensing the full $3,000 removes the unexpired portion from assets and cuts net income too much, so both assets and equity are understated at period end by that unexpired amount.

ww.Assets are overstated on the balance she: Assets are understated, not overstated, because the unexpired rent was expensed instead of being kept as a prepaid asset, so the balance sheet shows too little for assets.
ww.Liabilities are overstated at period end: The rent paid has no effect on liabilities, since no amount is owed; the error involves expensing too much, which understates assets and equity rather than overstating liabilities.
ww.Equity is overstated on the balance shee: Equity is understated, not overstated, because expenses were too high and net income too low; recording rent as an expense instead of an asset reduces equity.

rw: Supplies used equals $900 minus $350, which is $550, so debit Supplies Expense $550 and credit Supplies $550, leaving $350 of supplies on hand as an asset.

ww.No entry is needed for the supplies on h: A count shows only $350 left of $900, so $550 has been used up; no entry would leave supplies and expenses misstated for the period, so an entry is needed.
ww.Debit Supplies $550, credit Supplies Exp: This entry reverses the right accounts: it would increase Supplies and reduce expense, but $550 was used, so supplies should decrease and Supplies Expense should increase instead.
ww.Debit Supplies Expense $350, credit Supp: $350 is the amount still on hand, not the amount used; the entry should record the $550 used ($900 minus $350), not the remaining balance of supplies.

rw: The accounting period concept divides a business's life into equal time periods, such as months, quarters or years, so results can be reported and compared at regular intervals.

ww.Only profitable periods are ever reporte: Both profitable and unprofitable periods are reported; reporting only profitable periods would be misleading, and the period concept requires showing results for every period regardless of outcome.
ww.A business reports only once, at closing: Businesses report at regular intervals throughout life, not only at closing; the accounting period concept exists so that owners and lenders get timely information in between.
ww.Periods must always be exactly one year: Periods can be months, quarters or years, and a fiscal year can run any 12 months; the concept requires equal periods, not periods fixed at exactly one year.

rw: A reversing entry is optional and made at the start of a new period to cancel an earlier accrual adjustment, which simplifies recording the later cash payment or receipt.

ww.An entry that closes the revenue account: Closing entries clear revenue and expense accounts at year end; a reversing entry does something different, as it cancels a prior adjusting entry at the start of the next period.
ww.An entry that cancels a customer's order: Canceling a customer's order is a sales matter handled outside the journal entries; a reversing entry is an accounting entry that undoes a previous accrual adjustment.
ww.An entry that corrects the trial balance: Trial balance totals are corrected by finding and fixing errors with correcting entries; reversing entries are unrelated to fixing totals and only undo earlier accruals.

rw: A correcting entry fixes an error discovered after posting by reversing the wrong accounts and recording the right ones, leaving a clear audit trail instead of erasing anything.

ww.A reversing entry type: A reversing entry cancels an earlier accrual at the start of a new period; it is an optional bookkeeping step and not the usual way to fix a mistake after posting.
ww.An opening entry: An opening entry records the starting balances of a new business or new set of books; it does not fix errors in transactions that were previously posted to the ledger.
ww.A closing entry: A closing entry transfers temporary account balances to equity at period end; it is part of the routine cycle and not a tool for fixing posted mistakes.

rw: The $180 should be in Telephone Expense, so debit Telephone Expense and credit Utilities Expense for $180, which moves the expense to the correct account without touching cash.

ww.Erase the original entry from the genera: Erasing entries destroys the audit trail and is not acceptable once posted; the proper method is a correcting entry that leaves the original and the fix visible in the journal.
ww.Debit Cash, credit Utilities Expense for: Crediting Utilities Expense is partly right, but debiting Cash is wrong because no cash moved; the bill was already recorded, so only the accounts debited need to be corrected.
ww.Debit Utilities Expense, credit Telephon: This entry moves in the wrong direction: it would debit Utilities Expense again and credit Telephone Expense, doubling the original error instead of moving the $180 to the right account.

rw: A bank reconciliation compares the company's cash book balance with the bank statement balance, finding differences like outstanding checks, deposits in transit, fees and errors on either side.

ww.Revenue with expenses for the whole year: Comparing revenue with expenses is what an income statement does to find profit; a bank reconciliation compares cash figures, not the results of operations for the year.
ww.Assets with liabilities at the year end: Comparing assets with liabilities is what a balance sheet does; a bank reconciliation is a cash control that explains the difference between two cash balances at a date.
ww.Two vendors' price lists, compared befor: Comparing vendors' price lists is a purchasing task; a bank reconciliation has nothing to do with prices and instead matches company cash records against the bank's statement.

rw: Deposits in transit are recorded by the company but not yet by the bank, so they are added to the bank statement balance to reach the true adjusted cash balance.

ww.Outstanding checks: Outstanding checks have been written but have not yet cleared the bank, so they are subtracted from the bank statement balance, not added to it.
ww.Bank service charges: Bank service charges are deducted by the bank and not yet in the company's books, so they are subtracted from the book balance, not added to the bank balance.
ww.NSF returned checks: NSF returned checks are customer checks that bounced, and the bank deducted them, so they are subtracted from the book balance rather than added to the bank statement balance.

rw: Outstanding checks have been recorded by the company but not yet cleared by the bank, so they are subtracted from the bank balance to match the true available cash.

ww.Bank collections: Bank collections, such as notes collected on the company's behalf, increase the book balance side of the reconciliation, not the adjustments made to the bank statement balance.
ww.Deposits in transit: Deposits in transit are already in the company's books but not yet at the bank, so they are added to the bank statement balance, not subtracted from it.
ww.Interest earned: Interest earned is credited by the bank and is added to the book balance, because the company has not recorded it yet; it is not a subtraction from the bank balance.

rw: The bank takes the money back, so the company reduces Cash and re-establishes the customer's Accounts Receivable, because the customer still owes the amount for the sale or invoice.

ww.Increase cash by the same amount: An NSF check does not increase cash; the deposit is reversed because the funds never arrived, so the book balance must decrease, not increase, by the check amount.
ww.Decrease payables by the same sum: Payables are what the company owes its suppliers and are not affected by a customer's bounced check; the entry involves cash and the customer's receivable instead.
ww.Decrease revenue by the same amount: Revenue was already properly earned from the sale, and the bounced check does not undo the sale; the customer still owes the money, so revenue is not reduced by it.

rw: A petty cash fund pays small, routine expenses such as postage, coffee or office supplies, avoiding the need to write a formal check for each minor cost.

ww.Repaying bank loans: Repaying bank loans is done by regular check or bank transfer from the main account, since loan payments are large and need proper records, which petty cash is not designed for.
ww.Buying large equipment: Large equipment purchases go through purchase orders and the regular bank account with proper approval; petty cash holds a small sum and is not suited to big purchases.
ww.Paying staff salaries: Staff salaries are paid through payroll by check or direct deposit with tax withholdings recorded; petty cash is not meant for such large, regular and documented payments.

rw: Cash should be $200 minus $145 of receipts, which is $55, but only $52 is on hand, so the fund is $3 short, recorded as a debit to Cash Short and Over.

ww.$7 short: A $7 shortage would require only $48 in cash, but the expected cash is $200 minus $145, or $55, and $52 is on hand, so the shortage is $3.
ww.$3 over: Over means more cash than expected; expected cash is $55 and only $52 is on hand, which is less, so the fund is short rather than over by $3.
ww.All correct: The fund does not balance: receipts of $145 plus cash of $52 equal $197, not the $200 fund, so the $3 difference means the books are not all correct.

rw: The purchase would add $4,000 to equipment (asset) and $4,000 to accounts payable (liability), so leaving it out understates both assets and liabilities by $4,000 each.

ww.There is no effect because the equation: The equation still balances because both sides are understated equally, but that does not mean there is no effect; the totals for assets and liabilities are each wrong.
ww.Assets are understated, liabilities are: Liabilities are understated, not overstated, because the unrecorded purchase on account would have added a $4,000 payable; assets are also understated by the missing equipment.
ww.Assets and equity are both understated b: The purchase was on account, so it creates a liability, not a change in equity; equity is unaffected by buying equipment on credit, only assets and liabilities are.

rw: The cycle runs journalize, post, trial balance, adjust, prepare statements, then close, which follows the logical flow from raw transactions to final reports and a reset of temporary accounts.

ww.Prepare statements, journalize, post, th: Statements cannot be prepared before journalizing and posting, since they draw on ledger balances; closing the books also belongs after the statements, so this order is backwards.
ww.Close, journalize, post, adjust, then pr: Closing comes at the end of the cycle, not before journalizing, posting and adjusting; closing first would erase balances before the statements could report them accurately.
ww.Post, adjust, journalize, close, then pr: Posting requires journalizing first, since posting transfers journal entries to the ledger; this order puts post before journalize, which is impossible, and closes too early.

rw: An account balance is the difference between total debits and total credits; a positive result is a debit balance and a negative result is a credit balance.

ww.The number of entries posted to the acco: The number of entries posted is a count and says nothing about the amount in the account; the balance is a dollar figure computed from the debit and credit totals.
ww.The total of all entries, ignoring the s: Adding all entries regardless of side would produce a meaningless total, because debits and credits move the balance in opposite directions and must be netted against each other.
ww.The date of the last entry in the accoun: The date of the last entry is just a posting reference; a ledger balance is a dollar amount showing the net of debits and credits in the account.

rw: A debit is an entry on the left side of an account; it increases assets and expenses and decreases liabilities, equity and revenue under double-entry bookkeeping.

ww.Money paid to the owner each period: Money paid to the owner is called a withdrawal or drawing, which is a specific account; a debit is simply the left side of an account, not a payment to anyone.
ww.A request for payment sent to a customer: A request for payment sent to a customer is an invoice or bill; in accounting a debit is not a document but an entry recorded on the left side.
ww.An entry on the right side of an account: An entry on the right side of an account is a credit, which is the opposite of a debit; debits always go on the left side of the T account.

rw: A credit is an entry on the right side of an account; it increases liabilities, equity and revenue and decreases assets and expenses under double-entry bookkeeping.

ww.A loan from a bank to a customer firm: A loan from a bank to a customer firm is a type of credit extended, but in bookkeeping a credit is an entry, not a loan, on the right side.
ww.A discount offered to a buyer by a selle: A discount offered to a buyer is a sales or cash discount, which is a pricing term; the accounting meaning of credit is the right side of an account entry.
ww.An entry on the left side of an account: An entry on the left side of an account is a debit, the opposite of a credit; credits always go on the right side of the T account.

rw: The balance is debits minus credits: $12,000 minus $8,400 is $3,600, and because debits exceed credits it is a debit balance, normal for the Cash asset account.

ww.$8,400 debit: $8,400 is only the total of the credits, not the balance; the balance is the net of $12,000 debits and $8,400 credits, which is $3,600.
ww.$3,600 credit: Debits are larger than credits ($12,000 versus $8,400), so the $3,600 difference is a debit balance, not a credit balance, which would be abnormal for cash.
ww.$20,400 debit: $20,400 adds debits and credits together, but a balance nets them against each other by subtracting; $12,000 minus $8,400 gives $3,600 debit, not the sum.

rw: A subsidiary ledger holds the detail, such as each customer's account, behind a control account in the general ledger, whose balance should equal the subsidiary ledger total.

ww.To store old financial statements for au: Old financial statements are kept in archives or files for audits; a subsidiary ledger instead holds detailed accounts, such as individual customers, that support a control account in the general ledger.
ww.To record the owner's personal transacti: The owner's personal transactions should be kept separate from the business under the separate entity concept, and a subsidiary ledger deals with business details, not personal matters.
ww.To replace the general journal and ledge: A subsidiary ledger supports the general ledger and does not replace it, since the general journal and general ledger are still needed for the complete double-entry record.

rw: The control account and subsidiary ledger should agree, so the $450 difference ($18,500 minus $18,050) signals an error, and the bookkeeper should look for a posting or addition mistake.

ww.Delete the customer accounts from the bo: Deleting customer accounts would destroy valid records of amounts owed and not fix anything; the difference should be traced, not wiped out by removing accounts from the books.
ww.Adjust the control account without check: Changing the control account without finding the cause only hides the problem, and the real error would stay in either the subsidiary ledger or the control account postings.
ww.Ignore it because the difference is smal: Even small differences mean the records disagree and may hide a real posting error or fraud, so a $450 gap between ledgers should never be ignored just because it seems small.

rw: The explanation briefly describes the transaction in words, making the entry understandable to anyone who reads the journal later and supporting the audit trail for each transaction.

ww.To hide the transaction from auditors: Hiding transactions from auditors is improper; the explanation actually supports auditors by documenting why each entry was made, which makes the books more transparent and reviewable.
ww.To calculate the account balance: Account balances are calculated from the debit and credit amounts in the ledger, not from the narration, which is only a written line of description under the entry.
ww.To check the trial balance totals: Trial balance totals are checked using the account balances in the ledger; the narration is a text description and has no role in checking whether debits equal credits.

rw: Cash (an asset) falls $500 and Rent Expense reduces owner's equity by $500, so both sides of the equation decrease equally and the accounting equation stays in balance.

ww.No effect on the equation at all: Paying rent does have an effect: cash decreases and rent expense reduces equity, so the equation changes, even though it stays in balance after the transaction is recorded.
ww.Liabilities rise by $500, assets stay: Paying rent does not create a liability; it is a cash payment for an expense, so liabilities stay unchanged while assets and equity decrease together by the payment amount.
ww.Assets increase by $500 in the period: Paying $500 reduces cash, so assets decrease rather than increase; there is no new asset received that would offset the payment made in cash for rent.

rw: A $750 sale on account adds Accounts Receivable (asset) and Sales Revenue (equity), so assets and equity both rise by $750 and the equation remains in balance.

ww.Assets and liabilities both increase: Liabilities do not change because nothing is owed by the business; a sale on account creates a receivable owed to the business, and revenue increases equity, not liabilities.
ww.Cash increases by $750 at the time: The sale was on account, so no cash came in at the time; the asset that increased is Accounts Receivable, and cash rises only when the customer pays later.
ww.Assets decrease by $750 in total: Assets rise by $750, not fall, because a receivable is created from the sale; a decrease in total assets would not match a sale that earns revenue.

rw: Accounts Payable is a liability, a permanent account whose balance carries forward from one period to the next and appears on the balance sheet, so it is not closed.

ww.Sales Revenue: Sales Revenue is a temporary account that is closed at the end of every period, so it is not permanent and its balance is reset to zero for the next period.
ww.Owner's Drawing: Owner's Drawing is a temporary account, closed to capital at period end, so it starts each new period at zero; it is not permanent like asset or liability accounts.
ww.Rent Expense: Rent Expense is a temporary account closed to Income Summary at period end, and it starts the next period at zero, so it is not a permanent account.

rw: Closing entries credit Rent Expense for its full balance and transfer it to Income Summary, so the temporary account has a zero balance and is ready for the new period.

ww.Owed: Owed describes a liability balance, but Rent Expense is a temporary account that is closed during closing entries, so it does not have any amount owed after closing.
ww.Prior: Prior balance does not apply because the closing entry removes the balance; the account starts the new period fresh rather than keeping last period's amount in it.
ww.Total: The total of the period's rent is moved to Income Summary during closing and does not stay in the account, so no total remains after the closing entries are posted.

rw: Accounts receivable is money customers owe the business for goods or services sold on credit; it is a current asset that is expected to be collected in cash later.

ww.Cash kept in the business bank account: Cash kept in the business bank account is an asset called Cash, not accounts receivable, which is specifically a claim for money owed by customers rather than cash on hand.
ww.Money the business owes to suppliers: Money the business owes to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability; accounts receivable is the opposite, representing amounts customers owe to the business.
ww.Money the owner has invested in it: Money the owner has invested is owner's capital, an equity account; accounts receivable is an asset arising from customers who bought on credit and have not paid yet.

rw: Accounts payable is the amount a business owes its suppliers for goods or services bought on credit, a current liability that is paid in cash when the invoice comes due.

ww.Money kept for emergencies in a reserve: Money kept for emergencies is a reserve or contingency fund, an asset; accounts payable is a liability, an amount owed rather than money the business has set aside.
ww.Money customers owe the business for goo: Money customers owe the business for goods sold is accounts receivable, an asset; accounts payable is the opposite, an amount the business itself owes to others.
ww.Money paid to employees each pay period: Wages paid to employees are recorded as payroll expense, and unpaid wages as wages payable; accounts payable specifically covers money owed to suppliers for credit purchases.

rw: An invoice is a bill from the seller that lists the goods or services sold, quantities, prices and the total amount due, and it is the basis for the buyer's payable.

ww.A receipt for cash paid on the spot by a: A receipt is proof of payment already made, while an invoice requests payment that is still owed, so this describes a receipt and not an invoice.
ww.A list of the company's assets and value: A list of the company's assets and values is an asset register or part of a balance sheet, not an invoice, which is a bill sent to a customer.
ww.A tax form filed by a business each year: A tax form filed annually is a return, such as the Form 1040 or 1120; an invoice is a commercial document between a seller and a buyer for a sale.

rw: A purchase order is the buyer's written request to a supplier for goods or services at agreed prices, authorizing the purchase before delivery and the later invoice.

ww.A bill sent by the seller later: A bill sent by the seller after the sale is an invoice, not a purchase order, which is created by the buyer before the goods are ordered.
ww.A receipt showing goods arrived: A receipt showing goods arrived is a receiving report, which documents delivery after the order; a purchase order comes first and is sent by the buyer to the seller.
ww.A check used to pay a supplier's bill: A check used to pay a supplier's bill is a payment document made after the invoice; a purchase order is the earlier request placed to order the goods.

rw: A credit memo is issued by the seller to reduce what a customer owes, for example after a return or pricing error, and it lowers Accounts Receivable.

ww.A document that raises what a customer o: A document that raises what a customer owes is a debit memo, the opposite of a credit memo, which reduces the customer's balance instead of increasing it.
ww.A reminder of an overdue bill from the s: A reminder of an overdue bill is a past-due notice or statement; a credit memo is an adjustment document that lowers the amount owed by the customer.
ww.A form for applying for a bank loan or c: An application for a bank loan or credit is a credit application, a customer or borrower form; a credit memo is the seller's document reducing a balance owed.

rw: Net 30 means the full invoice amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date, giving the buyer a month of credit without any early payment discount.

ww.Payment is due in 30 hours or less: Net 30 refers to days, not hours; it says the full invoice amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date, with no early payment discount offered.
ww.A 30 percent discount applies: Net 30 does not mean a discount; discounts appear in terms such as 2/10, n/30, where the number before the slash is the percent discount offered for early payment.
ww.The invoice is for exactly $30: The 30 refers to the payment period in days, not a dollar amount; the invoice can be for any amount, and the buyer has 30 days to pay in full.

rw: Terms of 2/10, n/30 give a 2 percent discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date.

ww.Payment is due in either 2 or 10 days: The terms give a discount window and a full payment deadline, not a choice of two due dates; the buyer must pay by day 30, with a discount only before day 10.
ww.A $2 charge on the 10th day of the month: The 2 is a percent discount rate, not a dollar charge, and the 10 is a number of days, so the terms are not about a fee on the 10th day.
ww.A 10 percent discount if paid within 2 d: The discount is 2 percent, not 10, and the window is 10 days, not 2, so this reverses the numbers in the 2/10, n/30 terms.

rw: Day 8 is within the 10-day discount period, so the buyer takes 2 percent off: $2,000 times 0.02 is $40, and $2,000 minus $40 equals $1,960.

ww.$1,940: $1,940 would be a 3 percent discount, but the terms offer 2 percent, which is $40 off $2,000, so the buyer pays $1,960 rather than this amount.
ww.$1,800: $1,800 would be a 10 percent discount, which is much larger than the 2 percent offered in the terms, so the buyer would not pay this on day 8.
ww.$2,000: $2,000 is the full price, but paying on day 8 is within the 10-day discount period, so the buyer takes 2 percent off and pays less than the full amount.

rw: Day 20 is past the 10-day discount period, so the discount is lost and the buyer pays the full $1,500 invoice, which is due by day 30 under the n/30 terms.

ww.$1,350: $1,350 would be a 10 percent discount, but the terms offer 1 percent only within 10 days, and day 20 is outside that window, so no discount applies.
ww.$1,485: $1,485 applies the 1 percent discount ($15) to $1,500, but that discount is only allowed through day 10, and the buyer paid on day 20.
ww.$1,515: $1,515 adds 1 percent as a penalty, but the terms do not charge a late fee before day 30; the buyer owes the full $1,500 on day 20, with no add-on.

rw: A credit sale increases the asset Accounts Receivable with a debit of $600 and records the earned revenue with a credit to Sales Revenue of $600.

ww.Debit Sales Revenue, credit Accounts Rec: This entry reverses the sale: debiting Sales Revenue and crediting Accounts Receivable would reduce revenue and the receivable, which is what a sales return looks like, not a sale.
ww.Debit Cash and credit Accounts Receivabl: Debit Cash and credit Accounts Receivable records a customer paying what they owe, not the sale itself, and no cash is received at the time of a credit sale.
ww.Debit Accounts Payable, credit Sales Rev: Accounts Payable is what the business owes suppliers, so debiting it for a sale makes no sense; the debit should go to Accounts Receivable, the amount customers owe.

rw: The customer's payment increases Cash with a debit of $600 and decreases Accounts Receivable with a credit of $600, since the amount owed is now settled.

ww.Debit Cash and credit Sales Revenue: Crediting Sales Revenue would count the same sale again as new income; the revenue was recorded when the sale was made on account, so the payment should credit the receivable.
ww.Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Cash: Debiting Accounts Receivable and crediting Cash is backwards; it would increase what customers owe and reduce cash, instead of collecting a payment from the customer.
ww.Debit Accounts Payable, credit Cash: Accounts Payable concerns amounts the business owes its suppliers; a customer paying the business affects Accounts Receivable, so debiting Payable and crediting Cash does not fit.

rw: Buying inventory on account increases the asset Inventory with a $900 debit and creates a liability, Accounts Payable, with a $900 credit until the bill is paid.

ww.Debit Accounts Payable, credit Inventory: Debiting Accounts Payable and crediting Inventory would reduce a liability and an asset, which resembles returning goods, not buying inventory on account for $900.
ww.Debit Inventory, credit Cash for $900: The purchase was on account, so no cash was paid; crediting Cash would wrongly reduce the cash balance by $900, when the business instead created a payable.
ww.Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Invent: Accounts Receivable is what customers owe the business, so it does not belong in a purchase from a supplier; the liability created here is Accounts Payable.

rw: Paying down a supplier debt reduces the liability Accounts Payable with a debit of $900 and reduces the asset Cash with a credit of $900.

ww.Debit Inventory, credit Cash for $900: Debiting Inventory would count the goods twice, since inventory was already recorded when purchased on account; paying the bill only settles the payable, it adds no inventory.
ww.Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Cash: Accounts Receivable is money customers owe the business; this payment goes to a supplier, so the debit belongs in Accounts Payable, not in Accounts Receivable.
ww.Debit Cash, credit Accounts Payable: Debiting Cash and crediting Accounts Payable would increase cash and increase the liability, which is the opposite of paying a supplier $900 that is owed.

rw: An aging report sorts accounts receivable by how many days each invoice has gone unpaid, such as 1-30, 31-60 and over 90 days, showing which accounts are most at risk.

ww.A report of the owner's retirement plans: The owner's retirement plans have nothing to do with receivables; an aging report is a tool for managing money customers owe, based on how long invoices have been unpaid.
ww.A report of how old each asset is in yea: How old assets are in years describes an asset age or depreciation schedule; an aging report instead groups customer invoices by how many days they are past due.
ww.A report that lists all employees by age: Listing employees by age is a human resources report; an aging report in accounting groups unpaid customer invoices into categories like current, 30, 60 and 90 days.

rw: An aging schedule shows which customers are overdue so collection efforts can be targeted, and older balances are more likely uncollectible, which supports estimating the bad debt allowance.

ww.To list the company's suppliers by name: A supplier list is kept in vendor records and has nothing to do with customer receivables; an aging schedule of receivables is built from what customers owe, not who the suppliers are.
ww.To decide the owner's salary for the yea: The owner's salary is a management decision unrelated to receivables; an aging schedule is used for collections and bad debt estimates on customer accounts.
ww.To calculate depreciation on equipment e: Depreciation on equipment is calculated from asset cost, life and salvage value; an aging schedule of receivables deals with customer balances and has no role in depreciation.

rw: A bad debt is a receivable that the customer cannot or will not pay, so it is an uncollectible account and a loss to the business, recorded as bad debt expense.

ww.A discount given to good customers: A discount given to good customers is a sales or trade discount, which lowers a price; a bad debt is an amount the customer owes but will not pay.
ww.A loan with a very high interest rate: A loan with a very high interest rate is just an expensive loan, not a bad debt; bad debts relate to customers who fail to pay what they owe.
ww.Money owed to a supplier, overdue: Money owed to a supplier that is overdue is a late payable, a liability of the business; a bad debt is a customer's unpaid receivable, which is an asset.

rw: The direct write-off method records bad debt expense only when a specific account is determined to be uncollectible, debiting Bad Debt Expense and crediting Accounts Receivable at that time.

ww.The allowance method: The allowance method estimates bad debts in advance with an adjusting entry, before any specific account is known to be uncollectible, so it does not wait for the write-off.
ww.Percent-of-sales method: Percent-of-sales is an estimating approach used within the allowance method; it estimates bad debt expense from sales before accounts are written off, so it is not waiting for a write-off.
ww.Aging method for debts: The aging method also estimates uncollectibles in advance using the age of receivables, as part of the allowance method, instead of waiting until an account is known to be uncollectible.

rw: The allowance method estimates bad debts in the same period as the related sales, applying the matching principle and satisfying GAAP for most businesses with significant credit sales.

ww.Direct write-off: Direct write-off records the expense only when an account is written off, often in a later period than the sale, so it does not match the expense to the related revenue.
ww.Reversal method: A reversal method is not a recognized approach for bad debts; reversing entries relate to accruals, not to estimating uncollectible accounts for matching purposes.
ww.The cash method: The cash method does not estimate bad debts at all, as it records revenue only when cash arrives, so there are no receivables to be uncollectible and no matching.

rw: The allowance for doubtful accounts is a contra-asset with a credit balance that estimates how much of Accounts Receivable will not be collected, reducing receivables to net realizable value.

ww.An asset showing money set aside for loa: An asset showing money set aside for loans misdescribes the account; the allowance is not a fund of cash and has nothing to do with the loans the business makes.
ww.A liability for customer deposits held i: Customer deposits held in trust would be a liability, but the allowance for doubtful accounts is not a liability; it is a contra account that reduces receivables.
ww.An expense account for unpaid wages and: The allowance is a balance sheet account, not an expense; the related expense is Bad Debt Expense, which is recorded on the income statement when the allowance is set up.

rw: Net realizable value equals accounts receivable minus the allowance: $40,000 minus $2,500 equals $37,500, the amount the company expects to actually collect from its customers.

ww.$40,000: $40,000 is the gross receivables before subtracting the allowance; net realizable value is the amount expected to be collected, which is lower because of the doubtful accounts.
ww.$42,500: $42,500 adds the allowance to receivables, but the allowance is a contra account that is subtracted, so net realizable value must be below $40,000, not above it.
ww.$2,500: $2,500 is just the allowance, the estimated uncollectible amount; net realizable value is the receivables balance less that allowance, which leaves a much larger figure.

rw: Bad debt expense under percent-of-sales is the credit sales times the estimated rate: $200,000 times 1 percent equals $2,000 recorded as expense for the period.

ww.$198,000: $198,000 is sales less 1 percent, which is a net amount and not the expense; the expense is only the uncollectible portion, 1 percent of $200,000.
ww.$200: $200 would be 0.1 percent of sales, a decimal error; 1 percent of $200,000 is $2,000, so the expense is ten times larger than this figure.
ww.$20,000: $20,000 would be 10 percent of $200,000, which is a decimal slip; the estimate is 1 percent, so the correct expense is $2,000, not $20,000.

rw: The estimate is recorded by debiting Bad Debt Expense and crediting Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, which matches the expected loss to the period of the sales without removing a specific account.

ww.Debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Receivabl: Crediting Receivable directly is the direct write-off entry for a specific account; estimating bad debt expense instead credits the Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, which is a contra asset.
ww.Debit Allowance for Bad Debts, credit Ca: Debiting the allowance and crediting Cash would reduce the allowance and cash, which makes no sense for estimating an expense; no cash is paid when bad debts are estimated.
ww.Debit Receivable, credit Bad Debt Expens: Debiting Receivable and crediting Bad Debt Expense would raise receivables and cut expense, the opposite of what an estimate of uncollectible accounts does to the books.

rw: Writing off $350 debits the allowance and credits Accounts Receivable by the same amount, so net receivables (receivables minus allowance) stay the same, and no change occurs.

ww.Goes to zero: Net receivables do not fall to zero; writing off one $350 account only removes that account from both receivables and the allowance, leaving the net figure on the others unchanged.
ww.Rises by $350: Net receivables do not rise, because both Accounts Receivable and the allowance decrease by $350, which cancels out in the net figure on the balance sheet.
ww.Falls by $350: Net receivables would only fall by $350 under the direct write-off method; under the allowance method the write-off reduces both receivables and the allowance, so the net is unchanged.

rw: A write-off debits the Allowance and credits Accounts Receivable, both balance sheet accounts, so it has no effect on net income in the period of the write-off.

ww.Net income increases in the same period: Net income does not increase because of a write-off; the expense was already recognized when the allowance was estimated, and the write-off only moves balances on the balance sheet.
ww.Net income decreases by the write-off: Net income does not decrease at write-off, because the bad debt expense was already recorded when the allowance was set up; the write-off just debits the allowance.
ww.Revenue decreases in the same period: Revenue is not reduced by a write-off under the allowance method; revenue was recorded at the time of the sale, and the loss is handled through the allowance account instead.

rw: The business first reverses the write-off (debit Accounts Receivable, credit Allowance) and then records the collection (debit Cash, credit Accounts Receivable), keeping a full record of the customer's history.

ww.Record the cash as a new liability: The payment is cash received, not a loan or borrowing, so recording a new liability would be wrong; the business is recovering a receivable it had given up on earlier.
ww.Record revenue for the amount received: Revenue was already recorded at the original sale, so recording revenue again would double count it; the recovery just reinstates the receivable and records the cash collected.
ww.Ignore the payment from the customer: Ignoring the payment would leave cash and the records wrong; the business must record the recovery, even though the account was earlier written off as uncollectible.

rw: A note receivable is a customer's written promise to pay a specific sum, usually with interest, by a stated date, and it is an asset for the business that holds it.

ww.A written promise by the business to pay: A written promise by the business to pay a lender is a note payable, a liability; a note receivable is a promise made to the business by someone else.
ww.A reminder to the accounting team each m: A reminder to the accounting team has nothing to do with notes receivable; a note is a formal written promise to pay money, carrying a maturity date and an interest rate.
ww.A list of unpaid customer invoices to da: A list of unpaid customer invoices is an accounts receivable listing; a note receivable is a more formal written promise to pay, often with interest, signed by the customer.

rw: Interest equals principal times rate times time: $5,000 times 0.06 times 1 year equals $300, which is the cost of borrowing the money for the year.

ww.$5,300: $5,300 is the maturity value, which is principal plus interest; the question asks for the interest alone, which is the $300 added on top of the $5,000 principal.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 would be 60 percent of $5,000, a decimal error; 6 percent as 0.06 gives $5,000 times 0.06, or $300 of interest for one year.
ww.$30: $30 would be 0.6 percent of $5,000, a decimal slip the other way; 6 percent of $5,000 is $300, ten times larger than this figure.

rw: Interest is $4,000 times 9 percent times 6/12 of a year, which is $360 times one half, or $180 for the six-month period of the note.

ww.$360: $360 is a full year of interest at 9 percent on $4,000, but the note runs for only six months, so the interest is half that, or $180.
ww.$36: $36 would be 0.9 percent of $4,000, a decimal slip; 9 percent of $4,000 for a half year is $4,000 times 0.09 times 0.5, which equals $180.
ww.$720: $720 would be 18 percent of $4,000 for a full year, or 9 percent for two years; for six months the interest is only $180.

rw: Maturity value equals principal plus interest, so $2,000 plus $100 equals $2,100, the total the borrower must repay on the due date of the note.

ww.$100: $100 is just the interest earned on the note; maturity value is the principal plus that interest, which is the total amount due at the end of the note term.
ww.$1,900: $1,900 subtracts the interest from the principal, but maturity value is principal plus interest, so it must be larger than $2,000, not smaller than the principal.
ww.$2,000: $2,000 is only the principal; maturity value also includes the $100 of interest, so the borrower pays $2,100 when the note matures, not just the original amount.

rw: Borrowing on a note increases the asset Cash with a debit of $8,000 and increases the liability Notes Payable with a credit of $8,000 owed to the lender.

ww.Debit Notes Payable, credit Cash: Debiting Notes Payable and crediting Cash would record repaying a note, not borrowing; on the day of borrowing, cash increases and a liability is created.
ww.Debit Interest Expense, credit Cash: Interest Expense is recorded as time passes and interest accrues; on the day of borrowing no interest has yet been incurred, and no cash leaves the business.
ww.Debit Cash, credit Sales Revenue: Borrowed money is not revenue, so crediting Sales Revenue would overstate income; the credit should go to Notes Payable because the business must repay the loan later.

rw: The adjusting entry debits Interest Expense and credits Interest Payable, a liability, because the interest has been incurred during the year but not yet paid in cash.

ww.Interest Revenue: Interest Revenue is income earned by a lender, but the business issued the note and owes interest, so it records an expense, not revenue, on the borrowing.
ww.Notes Receivable: Notes Receivable is an asset for a lender holding a note; the issuer of the note owes interest and a liability, so crediting Notes Receivable would not make sense.
ww.Cash received: No cash is received or paid when interest is only accrued at year end, so the credit cannot go to Cash; it goes to a liability account instead.

rw: A vendor is a supplier from whom the business buys goods or services, often on credit, creating an account payable until the vendor is paid in cash.

ww.A customer who buys from the firm monthl: A customer buys from the firm, whereas a vendor sells to the firm; confusing them reverses the direction of the transaction between the two parties in a purchase.
ww.The owner of the business and its shares: The owner of the business and its shares is a proprietor or shareholder, not a vendor; a vendor is an outside party that supplies the business with goods or services.
ww.An employee who sells products in a shop: An employee who sells products is a salesperson, who works for the business; a vendor is an outside company or person that sells to the business.

rw: A receiving report records the goods that actually arrived, with quantities and condition, and is compared with the purchase order and invoice before the bill is paid.

ww.A bill for goods sent to a buyer: A bill for goods sent to a buyer is an invoice from the seller; a receiving report is created by the buyer's own receiving department on delivery.
ww.A record of goods ordered by us: A record of goods ordered by the buyer is a purchase order, which comes before delivery; a receiving report instead documents the goods that actually showed up.
ww.A list of payments received: A list of payments received is a cash receipts record or deposit listing; a receiving report relates to goods delivered to the buyer from a supplier.

rw: A three-way match compares the purchase order, the receiving report and the vendor invoice, so the company pays only for goods actually ordered and received at the agreed price.

ww.Matching debits, credits and all balance: Matching debits, credits and balances describes checking a trial balance, not the three-way match, which compares three specific purchasing documents before paying a vendor.
ww.Having three managers sign each check is: Three signatures on each check would be an approval control, but a three-way match refers to three documents compared, not three managers signing off on a payment.
ww.Matching three customers with three invo: A three-way match compares purchasing documents, not customers; three customers matched with three invoices would be a receivables task unrelated to verifying a vendor's bill.

rw: Separation of duties stops one person from both approving and paying a bill, so a fake invoice would need a second person's cooperation, reducing the chance of fraud.

ww.It speeds up payment to the vendor: Splitting the work between two people tends to slow the process slightly, not speed it up; the point is control and fraud prevention, not faster payment.
ww.It is required by every bank by law: Banks do not require this by law for every account; it is an internal control practice companies adopt to reduce errors and fraud, not a universal legal requirement.
ww.It makes the checks cheaper to print: Printing cost has nothing to do with who approves invoices and who signs checks; the reason is internal control, specifically separation of duties to reduce the risk of fraud.

rw: Only 90 units arrived, so the company should resolve the discrepancy with the vendor and pay for what was received, rather than pay for 100 units that were not delivered.

ww.Ignore the invoice and pay it in full la: Ignoring the invoice would damage the vendor relationship and leave a real payable unresolved; the discrepancy should be handled promptly instead of being paid later without any follow up.
ww.Pay for 110 units to be safe and keep th: Paying for 110 units makes no sense because only 90 were received and 100 were billed; overpaying wastes company money and does not resolve the discrepancy at all.
ww.Pay the full invoice now and ask for a f: Paying in full first means paying for 10 units never delivered, and getting the money back later is harder; the discrepancy should be settled before payment is made.

rw: Accounts Payable normally has a credit balance, so a debit balance usually means the company overpaid a supplier or a return or credit memo has not yet been applied.

ww.A new loan from the bank for the firm: A new bank loan would create a credit balance in a liability such as Notes Payable; a debit balance in Accounts Payable is unusual and means the company overpaid.
ww.Revenue earned but not yet billed: Revenue earned but not billed would be an accrued receivable or unbilled revenue, an asset; it has no connection to a debit balance in the Accounts Payable account.
ww.A normal amount owed to suppliers: A normal amount owed to suppliers shows up as a credit balance in Accounts Payable; a debit balance is the opposite and signals something unusual, such as an overpayment.

rw: Returning goods bought on account reduces the liability, so debit Accounts Payable $200, and credit Purchases Returns and Allowances to reduce the cost of purchases by the same amount.

ww.Debit Cash and credit Accounts Payable f: Debiting Cash would mean receiving money, but returning goods on account only cancels part of what is owed; crediting Accounts Payable would instead raise the liability, the wrong direction.
ww.Debit Purchases and credit Accounts Paya: Debiting Purchases and crediting Accounts Payable records a new purchase on account, which increases what is owed, whereas a return reduces the liability and the purchases.
ww.Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Invent: Accounts Receivable is what customers owe the business, so it does not apply to returning goods to a supplier; the debit should reduce Accounts Payable, the amount owed.

rw: A customer return reduces revenue through the contra account Sales Returns and Allowances (debit) and reduces what the customer owes by crediting Accounts Receivable by $150.

ww.Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Sales: Debiting Accounts Receivable would increase what the customer owes, and crediting Sales Returns would reduce the contra account, which is the reverse of what a return does.
ww.Debit Cash and credit Accounts Receivabl: The goods were bought on account, so no cash is refunded; crediting Cash is wrong, and the debit to Cash would also increase cash rather than reduce the receivable.
ww.Debit Sales Revenue and credit Cash for: Debiting Sales Revenue directly and crediting Cash assumes a cash refund; the purchase was on account, so no cash is paid, and the contra account tracks returns separately.

rw: The Allowance for Doubtful Accounts is a contra-asset, so it is subtracted from Accounts Receivable on the balance sheet, reducing receivables to the amount expected to be collected.

ww.The allowance increases receivables on t: The allowance reduces receivables because it is a contra account with a credit balance; it does not increase them, so this statement has the effect backward.
ww.The allowance is a revenue account on th: The allowance is a balance sheet contra-asset, not a revenue account; the related Bad Debt Expense appears on the income statement, but the allowance itself does not.
ww.The allowance shows on the income statem: Revenue appears on the income statement, but the allowance is a balance sheet account that reduces receivables; it is never reported as revenue by the business at all.

rw: The aging method sets the ending allowance at $4,200, and with a $700 credit balance already there, the adjustment is $4,200 minus $700, which equals $3,500 of expense.

ww.$4,200: $4,200 is the target ending balance of the allowance, not the expense; the existing $700 credit balance already covers part of it, so the expense is smaller.
ww.$4,900: $4,900 adds the existing credit balance to the target, but the existing $700 reduces the amount needed; the expense is $4,200 minus $700, not the sum.
ww.$700: $700 is only the existing allowance balance before adjustment; the expense is the amount needed to bring it up to $4,200, which is $3,500, not $700.
